cold: Day thirty. You've flown this plane two hundred times. In a simulator.
And the runway is not empty.
d01: Day one. Lakeshore International, the busiest airport in the Midwest.
You're eighteen. You throw suitcases for a living.
Flight nine-oh-two lands early, and the first passenger off bites the man checking his passport.
Ten minutes later, Terminal C is screaming.
You dive onto the baggage belt, ride it through the wall, and drop into the dark under the airport. Above you, every door locks.
d02: Day two. Something is sniffing your shoe.
A yellow Labrador in a blue vest that says K-9 Customs. Her tag says Pickles.
She's trained to find fruit in suitcases. She also finds you a sandwich.
Upstairs, every screen says the same thing. All flights cancelled. Airport closed. Stay where you are.
d03: Day three. You learn the airport has a secret.
Behind the walls, there are twelve miles of baggage belts. Tunnels, ramps and slides, under every gate.
They can't get in. The doors need a badge, and you have one.
You ride the belts everywhere. Pickles rides in a plastic tray. It's your own private subway.
d04: Day four. You learn the first rule by accident.
Your elbow hits the microphone at Gate A1, and your voice comes out of every speaker in the building.
Three thousand heads turn. And every one of them runs to Gate A1.
First rule: they follow sound. And you just found the loudest microphone in the Midwest.
d05: Day five. Duty free. You're filling a bag with chocolate when they come around the corner.
Nowhere to run. So you don't.
You stand perfectly still between two mannequins. Pickles sits. She doesn't blink.
They walk right past you. Close enough to smell.
Second rule: they don't see what doesn't move.
d06: Day six. Gate B4. A plane is still parked at the jet bridge, and its radio still has battery.
You put on the headset and say hello to nobody.
Somebody answers. This is Walt. Retired airline captain, seventy-two, on a dirt airstrip in Arizona with a parrot named Roger.
Nobody's coming for you, son. But I'm not going anywhere either. Eight o'clock. Every night.
d07: Day seven. One week alive deserves a hotel.
The first class lounge. Massage chairs. A shower with six kinds of soap. Free snacks that are actually free now.
Pickles sleeps on a leather sofa that costs more than your car.
In a crew locker, you find a pilot's jacket. It almost fits.
Best hotel in the Midwest. No other guests.
d08: Day eight. The toy store at Gate C2 has a remote control airplane.
You fly it down the empty concourse, over the moving walkways, around the dinosaur skeleton in the main hall.
Every one of them on the floor below follows the buzz. Like a parade.
You land it on the baggage carousel. Best day of your life. Remember the toy.
d09: Day nine. Walt has news. On day thirty, the quarantine zone gets sealed for good.
No trucks. No boats. No planes. Whoever is inside, stays inside.
Then I'll fly out, you say. You don't know how to fly, son.
The radio is quiet for a long time. Then: Roger that, says the parrot.
d10: The pilot training center has a flight simulator. A real one. It shakes, it tilts, and it screams when you crash.
Walt talks you through it on the radio. Pitch. Power. Breathe.
By midnight, you've crashed twenty-three times. Pickles has stopped watching.
d11: Day eleven. Dawn. You cross the tarmac to Hangar Nine, at the far end of the airport.
Inside, under a dusty cover, there's a little white plane with a red stripe. Four seats. One propeller. Her name is painted on the nose. Rosie.
Her battery is dead. Her tank is empty.
d12: Day twelve. In your locker, there's a postcard from your grandma June, in Kansas.
Fly safe, it says. She's never been on a plane in her life.
The phones are dead, so Walt calls her from Arizona, on a phone with a cord.
She says to eat a vegetable. And come home.
You hug Pickles for a long time.
d13: Day thirteen. The power flickers, and the baggage belts stop.
In the silence, you hear something you've never heard down here. Shuffling.
One of them found a way into the tunnels.
You run the belts backwards, slam the fire door, and stack suitcases against it until your arms shake.
Your private subway just got smaller.
d14: Day fourteen. You spell HELP on the tarmac with four hundred suitcases.
At noon, a helicopter comes over the trees. A news helicopter.
It circles twice. They film you waving. Then it flies away.
That night, you're on the news, Walt says. They're calling you the kid at the airport.
Nobody lands at an infected airport.
d15: You have a routine. Push-ups with a suitcase on your back. Pancakes at the diner, which Pickles steals. Simulator at noon.
Afternoons, you teach Pickles to sit in the co-pilot seat. She mostly sits in the pilot seat.
d16: Day sixteen. You climb the control tower for the first time.
From up here, you can see the whole airport. Three runways. Six hundred acres.
Thousands of them, wandering the taxiways like lost luggage.
And far away, beyond the fence, a line of lights that goes all the way around.
The army. Waiting for day thirty.
d17: Day seventeen. Rosie drinks avgas. Not jet fuel. Jet fuel would kill her.
The avgas tank is at the fuel farm, four hundred yards across open tarmac.
At two A.M., you drive a baggage tug across the field with twenty empty cans.
Halfway there, they hear the engine. You kill it. You freeze.
They pass. You push the tug the rest of the way.
d18: You search every gate, every bathroom, every tunnel.
You find her in Lost and Found. Ten thousand things nobody came back for. Teddy bears. A guitar. A wedding dress. A canoe.
She's asleep on a pile of stuffed animals.
Next to her, two pilot headsets, still in the box. Good dog.
d19: Day nineteen. Simulator. Crosswind. Low clouds. Night.
Walt doesn't say a word the whole time.
Touchdown. Gentle. Right on the centerline. Your first landing a passenger would actually survive.
For a second, the radio is silent. Then Walt says, that's a landing, son. And you hear him blow his nose.
d20: Day twenty. Second fuel run. This time, the tug dies halfway across the field.
And this time, they don't walk past. They see you.
Pickles barks once, and takes off running the other way. Every one of them follows her.
You push forty gallons of avgas to the hangar by hand.
She comes back at dawn, covered in mud, wagging. Rosie's tank is full.
d21: Day twenty-one. Rosie's battery is dead, so you jump-start her with the baggage tug.
Walt reads the checklist. Master switch. Mixture. Prime. Clear prop.
The engine coughs, catches, and roars. It's the loudest thing you've heard in three weeks.
By the time you shut her down, they're pounding on the hangar door.
d22: Day twenty-two. They don't leave. Two hundred of them, outside Hangar Nine, all night, all day.
You're trapped with a plane, a dog, and a toy airplane from Gate C2.
You fly it out the window, low, buzzing like an angry bee.
They follow it all the way to the lake.
Battery on the controller: one bar. Save it.
d23: Day twenty-three. You and Walt make the plan.
Rosie needs eight hundred feet of runway. Taxiway Kilo is three thousand. That's your runway.
At six A.M. on day thirty, the speakers play the final boarding call, and everyone in the terminal runs to Gate A1.
The toy airplane takes care of the rest.
Then full power. And don't look back.
d24: Day twenty-four. A thunderstorm rolls in off the lake.
Lightning hits the control tower. Every light in the airport goes out. And stays out.
No power. No speakers. No final boarding call.
Rain hammers the hangar roof all night.
Walt is quiet for a moment. Then he says, every airport has a generator, son. Go find it.
d25: Day twenty-five. The generator is three floors down, in a basement nobody has opened in three weeks.
It's dark, it's flooded to your knees, and it's not empty.
You fill the tank with diesel, pull the cord eleven times, and run.
Behind you, the lights come back on, floor by floor. The airport has a voice again.
d26: Day twenty-six. Walt sounds different tonight.
They moved it up, son. The zone closes at noon on day thirty, not midnight.
You'll get one try. One takeoff. If you abort, there's no second chance.
Then he gives you the last lesson. Don't fly the plane, son. Let her fly.
d27: Day twenty-seven. You record the boarding call.
Ladies and gentlemen, this is the final boarding call for flight thirty, to anywhere but here. Please proceed to Gate A1.
You set the timer for six A.M. Day thirty.
Then you write a note to Grandma June, and tape it inside Rosie's door. Just in case.
d28: Day twenty-eight. Midnight. Pickles growls at the fire door.
They're through. Into the tunnels, into the baggage hall, into everything that was yours.
You grab the headsets, the controller and the dog, and you ride the belt one last time, through the dark, all the way to Hangar Nine.
d29: Day twenty-nine. The last night. You sit in Rosie's cockpit with a flashlight and the checklist.
Pickles sits in the co-pilot seat, in a headset that's too big for her.
Outside, the rain stops. The stars come out over the runway.
Walt goes through every step with you, twice. Then he says, get some sleep, Captain.
d30: Every speaker in Lakeshore International says the same thing. This is the final boarding call. And three thousand of them run to Gate A1.
The hangar doors open. The toy plane buzzes the taxiway, and the last of them follow it to the lake.
Full power. Rosie rolls. They turn. They run at you. Eight hundred feet. Pull.
epi: Arizona. Walt is waiting at the end of his dirt strip. The parrot lands on your head.
A week later, Grandma June takes her first flight. With you.
